h1: The 6 Best Digital Magnifiers Under $500 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 handheld digital video magnifiers scored on zoom range, screen size, contrast modes and ease of use for low vision readers.
summary: The MoreDisp 5 inch is the one to buy for most readers: auto focus, 26 colour modes and simplified buttons. The RayHong goes furthest on zoom, up to 48 times. Eyoyo's 5 inch folds its handle into a stand for hands-free reading, and the smaller Eyoyo 3.5 inch is the pocket pick. All five are handheld video magnifiers, not microscopes or optical glasses.
intro: A digital magnifier is a tiny camera pointed at the page and a screen that shows it bigger. That sounds simple, and the trap is in the controls. A reader with low vision who has to hunt through menus to change contrast will stop using the device within a week, and the shelf is the most common place a magnifier ends up.

So we ranked six handheld video magnifiers by what a person with reduced sight actually has to do: focus, change colour mode, adjust zoom and hold the thing steady. We weighed zoom range, screen size, the number of contrast modes and how simple the buttons are, and left out microscopes and desk-lamp magnifiers because they solve a different problem.

products.name: MoreDisp Digital Magnifier 5 Inch, Electronic Auto Focus Reading Aid
products.verdict: Auto focus, 26 colour modes and simplified buttons on a 5 inch screen. The easiest to live with.
products.description:
MoreDisp pairs a 5 inch screen with electronic auto focus, 26 colour modes and a simplified button layout, and the listing names low vision and colour blindness as target uses. Auto focus is the quiet hero: manual focus on a handheld camera is fiddly for shaky hands.

It tops the ranking because ease of use is the thing that decides whether a magnifier gets used. The RayHong has a wider zoom range, but it asks you to find the right distance yourself, and the extra magnification is rarely used by ordinary readers. Against the Eyoyo 5 inch, MoreDisp trades the foldable handle for easier focus.

Buy it for reading mail, labels and menus. The caveat is that no zoom range is stated on the listing we reviewed, so check the figure before you order.
pros: Suits low vision and colour blindness
products.idealFor: Readers with low vision who want the simplest controls.
products.skipIf: You need the maximum possible magnification.

products.name: RayHong 5.0 Inch Digital Magnifier, 3X-48X Zoom Electronic Reading Aid
products.verdict: A 5 inch screen that zooms from 3X to 48X, with simplified buttons.
products.description:
RayHong offers the widest zoom in this ranking, from 3X to 48X, on a 5 inch screen with simplified buttons. It lists low vision and colour blindness among its uses, the same audience as MoreDisp.

It ranks just behind MoreDisp because most readers do not need 48X. High magnification on a handheld camera also exaggerates every tremor, so the image swims unless the device is propped on a surface. The upside is real for anyone reading fine print on medication or on circuit boards, where the extra range is not a gimmick.

Choose it for severe low vision or detailed work. The caveat is that high zoom and a hand-held device do not mix well, so set it on the page or a stand rather than holding it in the air.
products.idealFor: Readers with severe low vision or who read very fine print.
products.skipIf: You read standard print and want easy focus.

products.name: Eyoyo 5" Portable Digital Video Magnifier, 4X-32X Zoom w/Foldable Handle
products.verdict: A 5 inch screen with a 4X to 32X zoom and a handle that folds into a stand.
products.description:
Eyoyo's 5 inch magnifier zooms from 4X to 32X and has a foldable handle. The handle doubles as a stand: unfold it for carrying, fold it to rest the screen on the page. That makes it the better choice for long reading sessions.

It ranks third because MoreDisp and RayHong both list more on the accessibility side, with simplified buttons and listed low-vision targeting. The 4X floor is also higher than the 2X floor on the 3.5 inch Eyoyo, so it starts closer to the text. It is sold at a $100 to $200 price.

The pick for people who read for a stretch and want the device to stand on its own. The caveat is that the listing says little about colour modes or auto focus, so confirm both before you buy.
pros: Foldable handle acts as a stand
5 inch screen is easy to read
products.idealFor: People who read for long stretches and want a built-in stand.
products.skipIf: You want auto focus or simplified buttons.

products.name: Portable Digital Video Magnifier, Electronic Reading Aid 5.0 Inch with Foldable Handle
products.verdict: A 5 inch handheld with 2X to 32X zoom, 26 colour modes and a foldable handle.
products.description:
This unbranded 5 inch unit offers 2X to 32X zoom, 26 colour modes and a foldable handle, and the listing targets macular degeneration and low vision. On paper that combines the best features of the Eyoyo 5 inch and MoreDisp.

It ranks fourth because the feature list is long but the brand behind it is not named. It is also the only unit here in the $200 to $500 bracket, so you pay the most for a spec sheet that MoreDisp matches for less. The 2X start is lower than the Eyoyo 5 inch's 4X, which helps for a quick look at a label.

Buy it if the price gap does not matter and you want the foldable handle with many colour modes. Check the seller's return and support terms, as there is no recognised maker to call.
pros: 26 colour modes on a 5 inch screen
products.idealFor: Buyers who want colour modes and a foldable handle together.
products.skipIf: You prefer a recognised brand or a lower price.

products.name: Eyoyo 3.5" Portable Digital Video Magnifier, 2X-25X Zoom Reading Aid White
products.verdict: A 3.5 inch screen with 2X to 25X zoom, small enough for a pocket or purse.
products.description:
Eyoyo's 3.5 inch magnifier zooms from 2X to 25X and comes in white. It is the smallest and least expensive unit here, at the $50 to $100 mark, and the one you can carry to a restaurant or a pharmacy.

It ranks fifth because screen size is the limit. A 3.5 inch display shows fewer words at a time than the 5 inch models, so reading a page means more scanning and more fatigue. The upside is portability; the 5 inch units are noticeably larger to carry. Against the larger Eyoyo, you give up 7X of top-end zoom and nearly half the screen.

A good fit for spot reading: labels, menus, price tags. The caveat is that long reading on a small screen is tiring, so do not use it as your main device for books.
cons: Lower top zoom than larger models
products.idealFor: Spot reading of labels, menus and price tags on the go.
products.skipIf: You plan to read books or long documents.

products.name: Eyoyo 3.5" Portable Digital Video Magnifier, 2X-25X Zoom Reading Aid Black
products.verdict: The same 3.5 inch, 2X to 25X pocket magnifier as the white model, in black.
products.description:
This is the black version of the Eyoyo 3.5 inch magnifier, listed with the same 2X to 25X zoom and the same $50 to $100 price bracket. Nothing on the spec sheet separates it from the white model except the finish.

It ranks a step below the white version only because ties have to break somewhere, and the white listing came first in our review. Choose between them by colour and by which one is in stock. A darker body is less conspicuous in a bag, while the white model is easier to find on a pale counter.

It carries the same limits as its sibling: a 3.5 inch screen is a spot-reading tool, and a reader moving from the 5 inch MoreDisp will notice the smaller view at once. Skip both Eyoyo 3.5 inch versions if you plan to read pages of text.
pros: Same pocket size as white model
products.idealFor: Anyone who wants the pocket Eyoyo in a darker finish.
products.skipIf: You plan to read books or long documents.

methodology.title: Zoom range
methodology.description: The stated magnification from lowest to highest, since a useful range starts low for easy framing and reaches high for fine print.

methodology.title: Screen size
methodology.description: Display size in inches, because it sets how many words you see at once and how tiring a long read becomes.

methodology.title: Contrast and colour modes
methodology.description: The number and type of colour modes, which help readers with low vision or colour blindness find the best contrast.

methodology.title: Controls and focus
methodology.description: Button layout and whether focus is automatic, since this decides daily usability.

methodology.title: Handle and portability
methodology.description: Foldable handle or stand, size and price bracket for carrying and long sessions.

whatMatters.factor: Zoom range, low end and high end
whatMatters.detail: Zoom is how many times the camera enlarges text. A low floor such as 2X makes it easy to frame a page, while a high ceiling such as 48X helps with very fine print. Most readers live between 4X and 12X. Check both numbers on the listing, not just the maximum.

A bigger display shows more of the page and is easier on tired eyes. The jump from 3.5 inch to 5 inch is large in practice. Check the diagonal in inches on the listing, and be wary of units that quote only the overall dimensions of the device.

Modes such as white on black or yellow on blue can make text readable for people whose eyes struggle with black on white. More modes mean more chances to find the right one, but only if the button to change them is simple. Look for the mode count, as on MoreDisp, and a one-press switch.

A camera must be focused at the right distance to give a sharp picture. Auto focus does this automatically, which is a big help for shaky hands. Manual focus asks you to hold the right distance. Check the listing for the words auto focus before buying.

Holding a magnifier in the air amplifies hand tremor, especially at high zoom. A foldable handle or built-in stand lets the device rest on the page. If you plan to read more than a few lines, look for a folding handle in the title or photos.

faq.q: Does a digital magnifier replace reading glasses?
faq.a: No. A video magnifier shows a camera image on a screen, so it supplements glasses rather than replacing them. The MoreDisp and RayHong target low vision users who need more magnification than lenses give, but talk to an eye specialist about your needs.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake buying one?
faq.a: Chasing the highest zoom number. The RayHong reaches 48X, but at that level every hand tremor is magnified and the image swims. For most reading, a stable 5 inch screen with moderate zoom is more useful.

faq.q: Is the 5 inch screen worth it over the Eyoyo 3.5 inch?
faq.a: For anything longer than a label, yes. A 5 inch screen shows more words per view and tires the eyes less. The Eyoyo 3.5 inch is best kept for spot reading, where its pocket size is the benefit.

faq.q: How do I set one up?
faq.a: Charge the battery, switch it on, rest it on the page and pick a colour mode. On the MoreDisp, auto focus handles the sharpness. On the Eyoyo 5 inch, unfold the handle into a stand and adjust the zoom until the text feels comfortable.

faq.q: How do I look after a digital magnifier?
faq.a: Wipe the lens with a soft cloth, keep it dry and recharge it regularly. If the battery fades on the RayHong or any of these units, plug it in before you need it, because a flat magnifier leaves you with nothing.

faq.q: Can these double as microscopes or hobby tools?
faq.a: Not really. These are reading aids with modest zoom, built for text on paper. If you want to inspect coins or solder joints, a digital microscope is a different tool. For reading mail, the MoreDisp or Eyoyo 5 inch are better suited.

finalTake: The MoreDisp 5 inch is the digital magnifier to buy for most readers, because auto focus and simple buttons mean it actually gets used. Pick the RayHong when you need extreme zoom, the Eyoyo 5 inch for long sessions with its folding handle, and the Eyoyo 3.5 inch for the pocket. Rest the device on the page whenever you can, and your reading will be steadier.
